newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: Gulf capital markets lack depth - economist.
newsitem.headline: Gulf capital markets lack depth - economist.

text.p: Emerging stock markets in Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states are hampered by illiquidity and poor regulation and will have to work harder to attract foreign capital, a leading Gulf economist warned on Sunday.

"By emerging market standards, the Gulf stock markets continue to lack depth and versatility," Henry Azzam, chief economist at the Jeddah-based National Commercial Bank (NCB) told a meeting of bankers and investment houses in Abu Dhabi.

Market capitalisation in the GCC states of Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, United Arab Emirates, Oman, Bahrain and Qatar stood at $89.92 billion in 1996, representing an average of just 38.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), NCB figures showed.
Market capitalisation in the developed world typically stood at 80 percent of GDP, according to Azzam.
Out of total net capital inflows to all developing countries of $232 billion, only 0.6 percent or $1.4 billion was ploughed into GCC countries, mostly in the form of direct investment.
Share turnover also remained subdued in GCC markets.
"The total number of shares traded in 1996 did not exceed 20 percent of total shares outstanding in Saudi Arabia and the ratio was less than two percent in the UAE," Azzam said.
Shares in GCC markets were predominately owned by governments, family businesses and were mainly in financial companies rather than in manufacturing or other diverse sectors of the economy.
"By selling some state assets, governments of the region could create more companies whose shares are listed and traded on the stock exchanges thus adding depth and liquidity."
Even on the Gulf's biggest bourse, Saudi Arabia, capitalised at $45.3 billion, the state held 41 percent of shares.
A lack of legislation and market transparency and restrictions on foreign investment were also contributing to holding back market development in the six oil-rich states.

"A further factor inhibiting investment in the region is the dearth of uniform investment laws and regulations that make accounting, tax treatment as well as a proper legal framework for settling disputes accessible," Azzam said.
There were also a lack of market-makers, limited expertise in corporate bond issues and long-term bonds.
"The supply and flow of stocks available for investment should be increased and a wider participation in secondary market activities needs to be encouraged," Azzam said.

One way of increasing the role of the separate GCC exchanges was the creation of a single electronically linked regional exchange which would also be open to non-nationals resident in the GCC and then eventually to foreigners, he said.

"The small size of the region's stock markets should encourage the Gulf countries to push for shares to be listed and traded across boundaries, forming in effect a regional capital market," Azzam said.
